# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 22:56 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 90 active entries of tips_notebook.json (6 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot and the Village should scan for. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. A Lookout on the Katana holder sees nothing of the holder's attack, and killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that night. (seen in 3 games)
- Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique, and you must recheck who sent each PM and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can discredit a true claimant. (seen in 2 games)
- Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case. (seen in 3 games)
- Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one visitor can cover two targets (e.g. a Katana holder using their own action). List every way a count could fit before using it, and never hang on a count alone.

## Village
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 4 games)
- Two Sheriff claimants calling each other Evil can both be telling the truth, since Jesters and Executioners read Evil. Wait a day or find a mechanical check instead of hanging whoever sounded better. (seen in 2 games)
- Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them, and weigh these links above unverifiable late claims. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role. (seen in 5 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator just for having no results. (seen in 3 games)
- Keep a ledger of trial votes, announced totals, deaths and blocks. If a total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists: recompute the threshold, find the voter who matches every extra vote, and act before evil reaches half. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask everyone for a named suspect so you have a record, but a stack of echoed soft leans is not evidence. Watch for Yakuza nominating the pile-on target. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense. (seen in 2 games)
- When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.

## Yakuza
- Do the vote math in night chat. If your Innocent votes (plus a doubled ballot) can save a teammate, defend them; if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you. (seen in 6 games)
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited. Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict, and don't have two members claim Vanilla. (seen in 4 games)
- Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 3 games)
- After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 3 games)
- Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit. Never visit a suspected or claimed Veteran; hang them instead. (seen in 2 games)
- No Day 1 PMs between teammates, and give each teammate different wording; PM triangles and scripted lines become the town's lead for the whole game. (seen in 2 games)
- Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1. (seen in 2 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana. (seen in 4 games)
- You get no feedback, so never claim a confirmed save. Say your protection is consistent with the target surviving. (seen in 2 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot. (seen in 2 games)

## Veteran
- Alert on nights you drew attention, not quiet ones. Once you claim, Yakuza avoid you, so claim late and never reveal your remaining tokens.

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.

## Executioner
- Fake-claim Sheriff early with an Evil result on your target and a simple reason. Leading first makes their counterclaim look reactionary.

tips_feedback.tip: Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1.
tips_feedback.why: Yakuza recognized their numerical dominance once they reached 4 of 7 living players on Day 4, voting together in lockstep on Bob and Frank to close out the game cleanly.

tips_feedback.tip: Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role.
tips_feedback.why: Hiding my Oracle role early prevented an early N1/N2 assassination and allowed confirming Frank as Vanilla Villager in my will.

lessons.tip: A Tracker reports a destination, not the action performed there. If a tracked player visited someone who died to the Katana, that makes them a possible holder, but consider other visits and actions before calling it proof.
Keep nomination votes and trial votes separate. Account for the nominator's automatic Yes vote, and make clear whether your vote is a request to hear a defense or a judgment of guilt.
A role-block removes the blocked player's action; it does not stop another player from attacking the same target. Map each action and its effect separately before using blocks to rule out killers.

Track who repeatedly votes together on trials, especially when the cases are weak. A coordinated voting pattern across several decisions can be more informative than any one player's isolated behavior.

tips_feedback.tip: Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: The vote record showed Bob voted No on Carol's nomination of him, while his Yes votes on Heidi's nomination and his own nomination followed the stated rules. Checking the exact record exposed Mallory's accusation as a misread, though it did not change the outcome.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment.
tips_feedback.why: Bob correctly pointed out that Niaj's result established Heidi visited Alice, not that she used the Katana. A block could also explain a visit, so the tracker result alone did not prove the action.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions.
tips_feedback.why: Bob explained that nominating Heidi was a request to examine her unexplained knowledge, not a claim that she was already proven guilty. The distinction also mattered when his automatic Yes as nominator was mistaken for a contradiction.

lessons.tip: Before night actions lock in, explicitly count the votes needed for both Katana holder and target. Also check whether blocking the holder would stop the Katana attack, and whether changing the holder changes who visits the target.
Treat alignment checks as evidence about how a role appears, not proof of faction: list roles and effects that could produce the result, then seek independent corroboration before pushing a trial.
A Tracker result establishes a visit, not the visitor's exact action or motive. Combine it with attack and role mechanics, but keep claims proportional to what the result actually proves.

Track nomination votes separately from trial votes, and check the default-vote rules before alleging a contradiction. The nominator votes Yes on the nomination by default; missing trial votes count as Innocent.

In late game, calculate the strict-majority thresholds for both nomination and execution before acting. Coordinate votes around those thresholds, while avoiding claims about vote totals that the revealed ballot record contradicts.
Treat “Not Evil” as a narrow result, not a town-clear. Serial Killers and Arsonists read Not Evil, and the Katana holder can appear Good; keep those possibilities in your suspect pool.

Don't expose private night information in public unless you have a cover ready. Knowing that someone was role-blocked can reveal access to faction chat or a blocking role, even if you later claim another explanation.

A Katana attack is a visit and can identify its holder to a Tracker. If a Tracker may have checked you, consider moving the Katana before the next night and prioritize blocking or removing that Tracker.

Keep nomination and trial votes separate: a nomination can be a request to hear a defense, not a guilty verdict. Before voting Guilty, require a concrete fact that distinguishes guilt from an innocent explanation.

Treat role-block claims as conditional evidence. A block can rule out a killer's action only if the block actually happened; check who could know the result and whether the claim has independent support.

tips_feedback.tip: Sheriff: post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current.
tips_feedback.why: Dave followed the advice and revealed Carol's Evil result on Day 2. The Yakuza explicitly identified his Sheriff claim as an urgent threat and killed him that night; the result was also explainable by Carol's Ex-Con claim. Prompt disclosure can build credibility, but consider the danger when the result is ambiguous and your role is exposed.

tips_feedback.tip: Check mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: Bob correctly explained that he was Yes by default when Heidi nominated him and as the nominator of Heidi. Mallory treated those votes as a contradiction, but the revealed votes matched the rules and Bob's account. Careful ledger-checking exposed that accusation as unfounded, even though the majority still hanged him.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions; before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction.
tips_feedback.why: Dave nominated Carol but voted Innocent once her Ex-Con claim explained the result and no independent evidence emerged. That was the right distinction. Later, the majority ignored the same standard and executed Bob and Frank without a concrete case against either.

tips_feedback.tip: A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi used this ambiguity to recast Niaj's accurate report that she visited Alice as a Party Animal block rather than a Katana attack. Bob correctly noted the Tracker result alone did not prove which action Heidi performed; the rule gave the Yakuza a plausible way to muddy the evidence.

lessons.tip: When a player reveals information only a blocker or a Yakuza teammate could know, such as a private night block before it is announced, treat it as a strong lead. Check claimed night actions against visit logs and ask for a checkable detail rather than a restatement.

With Standard Defense, a Katana (Standard) cannot kill you; only Strong attacks, Divine attacks or a hanging can. Your real risk is the day vote, so plan for that rather than assuming the night is your only danger.

lessons.applies_to: Serial Killer and other Neutral roles
lessons.tip: Staying silent and letting Village hang the Yakuza is a losing plan when the Yakuza coordinate pattern-based nominations. Answer the specific case with a concrete counter-fact early, before trial day, and build a visible, checkable identity.
Day 1 was spent debating the process of Bob's prompt rather than sharing concrete reads. Move quickly to specific, revisable suspicions and vote on checkable facts so the day produces information.

Track which claimed role is consistent with night results and deaths: a public Tracker or Sheriff claim that the table can check against kills and blocks is worth more than vote-count arguments, so press for the specific night-by-night facts early.

When a player's knowledge seems to come from private information (e.g. knowing who was role-blocked), ask them to explain the source immediately and before any nomination; the slip is most useful while the player is still unsure what to say.

Avoid voting Yes on a nomination just to hear a defense; with few living players, a single Yes can combine with others to pass a nomination and hang a player on a thin case, so reserve Yes for players with a concrete reason.

lessons.applies_to: Heidi-type Party Animal or Pharmacist claims (Village blockers)
lessons.tip: Blockers should avoid revealing knowledge of a blocked player's action before the reveal, and should not claim a role that contradicts the public block log unless ready to defend it on the record.
Keep the Katana holder stable and avoid unnecessary holder changes at night, since moving the holder creates a visible visit and a split-vote risk that exposes the team to Tracker results.

Private-message contents are private, but who messages whom is public. Keep unnecessary PMs brief: repeated trust-building messages create a visible connection that can attract attention or become a target.
A result showing no visitors does not clear a player or prove they did nothing. Astral actions and self-only actions may not register as visits, and role-blocks can also prevent an expected visit.

lessons.applies_to: Trackers, Lookouts, and anyone using their results
lessons.tip: A visit result identifies a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. Treat it as a lead, then check whether other actions could produce the same visit before calling someone caught.

Check the exact ballot and the player's exact statement before calling a vote contradiction. Even a real inconsistency is a reason to ask questions, not proof of faction; an opponent can use a townie's slip to build a persuasive but false case.
Do not let a correct accusation against one threat certify its accuser. Reassess each trial independently; an opponent can help execute a real enemy to gain credibility for later pushes against town.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat nominations and trials as separate decisions; before voting Guilty, name a concrete contradiction rather than relying on a thin case.
tips_feedback.why: The town's caution on Carol's trial was understandable because Dave's Evil result fit her Ex-Con claim, but Carol was actually Yakuza and survived. The restraint benefited evil, though the tip remains sound guidance for avoiding unsupported executions.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep votes consistent with stated reads; check vote mismatches rather than overlooking them.
tips_feedback.why: Bob really did contradict himself about voting No on his own nomination, despite the tally showing Yes. That was worth checking, but the Yakuza turned the slip into a decisive case against a Vanilla Villager. A mismatch is a lead, not a faction verdict.

tips_feedback.tip: Every Yakuza member should submit Katana-holder and attack votes each night and confirm the plan.
tips_feedback.why: The Yakuza coordinated their holder and target votes throughout, moved the Katana successfully on Night 4, and paired attacks with role-blocks. They avoided a split or canceled attack and removed the remaining investigative threat.

lessons.tip: Silence is suspicious, but noise is also suspicious. Everry post should add one new checkable thing: a vote reading, a role claim, a timeline, or a question that forces someone else to commit to a fact. If you have nothing, say that in one line and stop. Long posts that just restate the obvious make you look like you are hiding behind text.

You do not have to use your action on night 1. If you investigate a player who is likely to die early or whose result will be messy, you waste your power. Watch day 1 for who is pushing, who is claiming, and who is being defended. A check on a loud suspicious player is worth more than a random check.

Killing a random person is rarely optimal. Kill someone who has claimed a role that threatens you, someone who is leading the town, or someone whose death creates confusion. If two killers both target the same player, you waste one kill. You cannot coordinate unless you can talk privately, so choose a target that is valuable even if someone else also hits them.

Do not defend your teammates too openly. If you always vote with the same people, or never suspect them, town will notice. It is okay to put a light suspicion on a teammate early, especially if they can defend themselves. You can always pivot later. Distance is safer than a solid voting bloc.

When someone claims a power role, ask what result they got and whether that result can be explained by another role. A Sheriff claiming Evil might be seeing an Ex-Con, a framed player, or a Yakuza with the Katana. Do not hang on one alignment check alone. Demand corroboration.

Track the Katana holder's visit as a visit to the target: a Tracker sees the holder visit the victim, so a holder who attacks a Tracker-visible target exposes themselves. Pick attack targets whose death leaves no Tracker or Lookout alive to read the holder's visit.

Never let a teammate's public or private claim contradict a logged fact the living Tracker holds. Heidi's Party Animal story (block on Alice N2 and N3) was contradicted by Niaj's visit log, so pick a cover story that is consistent with every visit that can be seen before committing.

A Sheriff or Oracle result is only as strong as its checkability; before voting Guilty on a claimant, ask which check remains independently verifiable (e.g. a fresh Tracker or Lookout log) and push for it rather than hanging on a single unverifiable check.

Watch who turns an unanswered question into a nomination and then votes on their own trial; a Yes-vote on one's own nomination and a claimed No-vote can both look like a contradiction, so verify the tally before pressing it.

Trials that pass with only the minimum Yes votes and a bloc of identical reasons are a warning sign; a Village that hangs its own power roles on thin reads (Erin, Bob, Frank) lets the Yakuza take the majority by attrition.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Our bloc kept consistent votes across trials, so the Village could not point to a mismatch on us.

tips_feedback.tip: Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi's Party Animal claim was checked against the living Tracker's visit log, which exposed the cover story and forced us into a late reactive plan.

tips_feedback.tip: After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them.
tips_feedback.why: Village players who used this read against Heidi and Carol in Day 4-5 pressed trials on the same bloc, which kept shifting the suspect pool toward the remaining villagers.

tips_feedback.tip: Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi's Day 4 and Day 5 claims of Party Animal blocks on Alice were checkable against Niaj's Tracker log, which the Village used to create the decisive contradiction.

lessons.tip: Strong vs Strong defense survives, and Standard defense does not stop Strong attacks. If you fear a Serial Killer or another Strong attacker, protect yourself or a key target with Strong defense (2 tokens), not Standard (1 token).

Never publicly mention a player was role-blocked unless your claimed role or public result justifies it. Only the blocker or an evil teammate would know, so prearrange a cover role and exact night story before using that info.

When checking vote contradictions, remember the nominator votes Yes by default and non-voters count No/Innocent. Don't treat a nominator's Yes as hypocrisy without checking whether they were the nominator.

The Katana attack is a visible visit by its holder. If a Tracker is alive, avoid letting the same holder visit multiple nights; move the Katana to a low-profile Grunt, or block/kill the Tracker before they can report the pattern.

If Mortician can clean kills, last wills may be hidden permanently. Share actionable results early in the Day and keep exact target/result in your will; a useful result is not useful if only a cleaned body knows it.

Each member should submit their Katana-holder and attack votes every night, then confirm the majority before resolution. Coordinate the role-block with the kill, and prioritize likely investigators or trackers over players with no apparent night action.

Treat every detail learned from faction chat or a teammate's action as dangerous to reveal publicly. If you disclose private night knowledge, have a mechanically plausible explanation ready immediately; unexplained knowledge gives the Village a concrete lead.
A Tracker result proves a visit and destination, not the visitor's faction or which action they performed. Check all mechanically possible explanations before treating a visit as proof of a kill.

In the endgame, calculate both nomination and trial thresholds before acting. When your faction has a voting majority, coordinate a reliable nomination and guilty vote rather than letting discussion create an avoidable split.

tips_feedback.tip: Yakuza: Every member submits their action and Katana vote each night; confirm the holder and target in chat.
tips_feedback.why: All four Yakuza coordinated their votes and actions, including unanimously transferring the Katana to Ivan on Night 4 while blocking and attacking Niaj. The clear quorum produced the kill and removed the Tracker.

tips_feedback.tip: Everyone: A visit shows a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment.
tips_feedback.why: Niaj's result established that Heidi visited Alice, but did not prove Heidi was Yakuza or that her visit was specifically the Katana attack. The ambiguity allowed Heidi's Party Animal explanation to remain plausible, even though the result correctly kept pressure on her.

tips_feedback.tip: Everyone: Keep votes consistent with stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Our public explanations matched our Guilty votes on Erin, Bob, and Frank. That consistency made our coordinated votes look like a continuous town read rather than a sudden change of position.

lessons.tip: Track voting blocs when mechanical evidence is ignored: if a player is caught visiting a murder victim and a solid 4-player bloc still pushes an execution on someone else, that bloc likely constitutes an evil majority controlling trial votes.
Target players who exhibit slips of private night information (such as revealing unannounced role-blocks); they are often the exact evil players carrying out kills or coordinating night actions.

Be vigilant about evil parity thresholds: at 7 players alive with 4 Yakuza, evil commands a strict majority (4/7) on nominations and trials, meaning town must identify and dismantle evil teams before reaching 7 alive.

summary: The Yakuza (Carol Puppeteer, Heidi Mortician, Ivan Grunt, Mallory Pharmacist) won by reaching a voting majority on Day 4 and hanging the last villagers. The decisive Village error came on Day 2. Dave's real Sheriff result, Carol = Evil, was dismissed 0-10 after Carol fake-claimed Ex-Con. Dave himself voted Innocent, and nobody planned a mechanical test of the claim. Mallory's Night 2 block on Alice stopped the one test that was coming: Alice's Oracle guess of Ex-Con on Carol, which would have come back wrong. Both evil factions then killed Dave, and the Mortician cleaned him, so his flip was hidden. On Day 3 Heidi slipped by naming Alice's private Night 2 block. Alice and Niaj caught it, and Erin pointed straight at it. Even so, Bob, who had just said he wouldn't hang Erin on that case, cast the deciding fifth Guilty vote on Erin (the Serial Killer). The town held 5 of 9 votes that day and could have hanged Heidi instead. The Yakuza killed Alice that night, which gave them 4 of 7 seats. Niaj held his Tracker log (Heidi visited Alice on Night 3) until Day 4, when it could no longer change a vote. Yakuza coordination was clean throughout: unanimous votes every night, sensible blocks, and a fallback Party Animal claim from Heidi. Their one real mistake was Heidi's slip, and the town failed to punish it.

lessons.tip: Don't acquit a Sheriff-confirmed Evil just because they claim Ex-Con, a role that exactly explains the result and can't be checked. Either hang them while the town still has numbers, or set up a mechanical test that night: a Tracker or Lookout on the claimant (an Ex-Con must visit someone every night), or an Oracle guess of Ex-Con. Then hang them the next day if the test fails.
lessons.evidence: On Day 2 Carol was acquitted 0-10, with the Sheriff himself voting Innocent. Carol was the Puppeteer. No Tracker was pointed at her, and Alice's planned Ex-Con guess was blocked. Carol survived to the end and won.

lessons.tip: When someone reveals night knowledge they shouldn't have, switch the day's hang to them right away. Vote Innocent on the current trial and nominate the slipper. Never let an older, weaker case keep your Guilty vote, and make your vote match what you just said.
lessons.evidence: On Day 3 Heidi stated that Alice was blocked on Night 2, which only the Yakuza could know. Bob said he wouldn't hang Erin on that case, then cast the fifth and deciding Guilty vote. The five non-Yakuza could have hanged Heidi instead.

lessons.tip: Count the evil votes every day. Once the Yakuza are one night-kill away from a majority, everyone with information must post it now, before the next night. Results revealed after evil holds the votes are worthless.
lessons.evidence: There were 4 Yakuza among 12 players. After Erin's hang and Alice's death, the Yakuza held 4 of 7 seats. Niaj posted 'Heidi visited Alice' on Day 4, but by then the Yakuza simply hanged Bob, and then Frank.

lessons.tip: Spend early checks on players who are active or under suspicion, or who claim a role, not on self-declared Vanillas or quiet players. A target that gives a confirmable result about a claim is the most valuable.
lessons.evidence: On Night 1 Alice spent her Oracle guess confirming Frank's own Vanilla claim, and Niaj tracked Vanilla Bob. Meanwhile Dave's check on the Day 1 nominator (Carol) hit a Yakuza.

lessons.tip: When an investigator catches a teammate, counterclaim the one role that fully explains the result (an Ex-Con for a Sheriff Evil). That night, use the Pharmacist to block the player most likely to test the claim, and kill the investigator.
lessons.evidence: Carol's Ex-Con claim turned Dave's Evil result into 0 Guilty votes. Mallory blocked Alice on Night 2, the night she guessed 'Ex-Con' on Carol. Heidi killed Dave and cleaned him.

lessons.tip: Never mention facts you learned from the night chat or the Yakuza action report in public. If you slip, kill whoever caught it that night, and prepare one consistent fake Village role (such as Party Animal) that explains the knowledge. Move the Katana off the exposed member.
lessons.evidence: Heidi's Day 3 slip about Alice's block nearly flipped the town. Killing Alice on Night 3, claiming Party Animal, and moving the Katana to Ivan on Night 4 contained it. Keeping the Katana with Heidi on Night 3 let Niaj track her visiting Alice.

lessons.tip: When the town is set to hang a rival Neutral killer, add your Guilty votes. It removes a threat to you, keeps your record clean, and spends the town's day on a non-Yakuza target.
lessons.evidence: All four Yakuza voted Guilty on Erin (the Serial Killer), which secured the 5-of-9 hang and used up the day the town should have spent on Heidi.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions... Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case.
tips_feedback.why: Dave, Alice, Bob and others treated a real Sheriff Evil result plus an unverifiable Ex-Con claim as 'no concrete contradiction' and acquitted the Yakuza Carol 0-10. Applied rigidly, the tip let a caught Yakuza go free.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays.
tips_feedback.why: Alice spotted Heidi's impossible knowledge of her Night 2 block, voted Innocent on Erin, and recorded the slip in her will. Not enough players followed it to change the result.

tips_feedback.tip: Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads.
tips_feedback.why: Bob, a tip recipient, broke it. He said he wouldn't support hanging Erin on the circumstantial case, then cast the deciding Guilty vote. That killed a non-Yakuza and pushed the Yakuza to a winning position.

tips_feedback.tip: Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat.
tips_feedback.why: Ivan and Mallory confirmed the holder and target every night. All four Katana votes were unanimous, and no kill was ever lost.

tips_feedback.tip: Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit.
tips_feedback.why: On Night 3 Ivan argued against this and kept the Katana with Heidi, and Niaj tracked Heidi visiting the dead Alice. Following the tip on Night 4 (Ivan as holder) left no further visit evidence on the exposed member.

issues.description: Day 4: Bob voted Yes on Heidi's nomination of himself, which put him on trial (5 Yes, 4 needed); his own vote was decisive. In his defense he then said he 'voted No on my own nomination' although the tally listed him Yes as nominator of Heidi. He later gave a muddled correction. This looks like confusion about the Yes/No interface and the nominator's default Yes, and it handed the Yakuza a 'checkable contradiction' that helped get him hanged.

R4 says the nominator 'votes Yes by default' but does not say whether the nominator can change that to No. Bob seemed to believe he had voted No on his own nomination of Heidi, while the log recorded him as Yes.

Night 2: Dave was killed by two successful attacks at once (Katana Standard and Serial Killer Strong). The rules don't say how a death with several sources is reported (cause in R12, attacker notifications in R3). The moderator flagged that the kill op takes only one cause/killer, then improvised a combined cause, 'Katana and Serial Killer', which was announced publicly. That public detail mattered later: it let players narrow down the SK.

Heidi's model (deepseek-v4.1-flash) hit finish_reason=length three times on Day 3, giving unparsable answers that needed retries. The truncated raw reasoning, including Yakuza strategy, was written into the log. The output token budget looks too small for this model, and leaked reasoning text should be kept out of any log players might see.

Day 3: Heidi said publicly and privately that the Serial Killer's Standard Defense means 'no Katana and no bullet removes them; only a hanging does'. A Vigilante's Strong shot (3 tokens) would kill an SK. Mallory and others accepted this misreading of the attack/defense rules without challenge.
